summary: Psalm 46 begins with confidence that God is refuge and help even if the earth, mountains, and seas collapse into chaos. It then turns to the city of God, where God’s presence steadies the city while nations rage. The psalm ends by inviting readers to look at Yahweh’s works, especially his power to end war, and repeats the refrain that Yahweh of Armies is with his people.
whyItMatters: This psalm gives one of the Psalter’s clearest images of trust under upheaval: the world shakes, nations rage, and God remains present. In Book II of Psalms, it belongs among Korahite songs that keep Jerusalem, worship, danger, and divine refuge in view.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with the sons of Korah and gives musical or performance information; psalm headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or performance setting.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms for public prayer and private use.
context.date: The Psalms are a many-period anthology; this chapter should not be assigned one certain date from this chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem imagines cosmic upheaval, international conflict, and the city of God with the holy place of the Most High.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with repeated refrain, vivid images of earth and sea, and the performance marker “Selah.”

outline.heading: God as refuge amid collapse
outline.note: The psalm opens with God as help in trouble and pictures earth, mountains, and seas in violent motion.

outline.heading: God within the city
outline.note: A river makes the city of God glad, and God’s presence within her keeps her from being moved.

outline.heading: Nations shaken, refrain of refuge
outline.note: Nations and kingdoms are disturbed, but God’s voice overpowers the earth; the refrain names Yahweh of Armies and the God of Jacob as refuge.

outline.heading: Come and see Yahweh’s works
outline.note: The audience is invited to look at Yahweh’s works, including desolations and the ending of war by breaking weapons.

outline.heading: God exalted, refrain repeated
outline.note: God speaks of being known and exalted among the nations and on the earth, and the psalm closes with the same refuge refrain.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. By the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
keyVerses.why: This opening line states the psalm’s central claim before the images of danger begin.

keyVerses.text: God is within her. She shall not be moved. God will help her at dawn.
keyVerses.why: This verse focuses the psalm’s trust on God’s presence in the city of God.

keyVerses.text: He makes wars cease to the end of the earth. He breaks the bow, and shatters the spear. He burns the chariots in the fire.
keyVerses.why: The verse shows that God’s power is not only defensive; it ends warfare and destroys its weapons.

keyVerses.text: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”
keyVerses.why: Here God speaks directly, moving the psalm from description to a command to recognize God’s rule over nations and earth.

themes: The city of God made glad

questions.question: Who are the “sons of Korah”?
questions.answer: The heading associates this psalm with the sons of Korah. Headings may name performers, collections, dedication, genre, or authorship, so this should be treated as real transmitted information without making a more specific claim than the text gives.

questions.question: What does “According to Alamoth” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the heading as part of the psalm’s musical or performance information. The chapter does not define the term. Its exact ancient force is uncertain, so readers can recognize the performance direction without reconstructing a precise instruction from it.

questions.question: Is the psalm saying natural disasters will not happen?
questions.answer: No. The psalm imagines extreme upheaval: the earth changes, mountains are shaken into the seas, and waters roar. Its claim is that the speakers will not be afraid because God is their refuge and help, not that the frightening events are impossible.

questions.question: What is the “city of God”?
questions.answer: The psalm describes the city of God as the holy place of the tents of the Most High. Many readers connect this language with Jerusalem and its temple, but the verse itself emphasizes God’s presence and the city’s gladness rather than giving a full geography lesson.

questions.question: Why does the psalm mention a river?
questions.answer: The river image contrasts with the threatening waters in verses 2-3. Earlier the waters roar and trouble the mountains; here the streams make the city of God glad. The chapter uses water both as an image of chaos and as an image of life and joy near God’s presence.

questions.question: What does “Yahweh of Armies” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the repeated refrain: “Yahweh of Armies is with us.” In this psalm, that title is tied to protection, refuge, nations in turmoil, and the ending of war. The chapter does not pause to define the phrase, but its placement presents Yahweh as the powerful God who is present with his people.

questions.question: Why does God make “desolations” if the psalm also says he makes wars cease?
questions.answer: This is a hard tension in the chapter. Verse 8 invites readers to see Yahweh’s works, including desolations, and verse 9 says he stops wars by breaking bows, shattering spears, and burning chariots. Readers differ on how to weigh the image: some stress judgment against violent powers, while others stress the frightening cost of God’s intervention; the psalm itself links the destruction of weapons with the end of war.

questions.question: Does “Be still” mean private calm or something larger?
questions.answer: The line can comfort an individual reader, but in the chapter it is addressed in a wider scene of nations, earth, wars, and God’s exaltation. The command is followed by “I will be exalted among the nations” and “I will be exalted on the earth,” so the immediate focus is recognition of God’s rule, not only inner quiet.

questions.question: Why is the refrain repeated?
questions.answer: The repeated line gathers the psalm’s confidence after scenes of upheaval and conflict. Verse 7 follows raging nations and a melting earth; verse 11 follows God’s declaration that he will be exalted. The repetition helps the reader hear the central assurance twice: Yahweh of Armies is with us, and the God of Jacob is our refuge.

glossary.def: A place of safety or protection. In this psalm, God himself is called the refuge of the speakers.
A term in the heading connected with the psalm’s performance or musical direction. Its exact force is not explained in the chapter.
A preserved performance marker in Psalms. Its exact instruction is no longer known.
The place made glad by a river and steadied by God’s presence in verses 4-5.
A title for God used in the refrain in verses 7 and 11, where it is connected with God being with the speakers.
